prescriptions.name: Acne Vulgaris
prescriptions.summary: Acne vulgaris is a common chronic inflammatory skin condition involving the pilosebaceous units. It commonly presents with comedones, papules, pustules, nodules, and scarring, often on the face, chest, and back. Treatment is tailored to severity and may include topical agents, oral antibiotics, and adjunctive skincare.

prescriptions.name: Doxycycline 100 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule once daily with food for 12 weeks

prescriptions.name: Azelaic Acid 15% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply thin layer to affected areas twice daily for 12 weeks

prescriptions.name: Benzoyl Peroxide 2.5% gel
prescriptions.sig: Apply thin layer to affected areas at bedtime for 12 weeks

prescriptions.name: Acne Soap (salicylic acid based)
prescriptions.sig: Wash face twice daily

prescriptions.name: Sunscreen SPF 30+
prescriptions.sig: Apply daily before sun exposure

prescriptions.notes: Combination therapy with oral antibiotic and topical agents. Counsel on potential photosensitivity with doxycycline; strict sun protection is essential. Expect gradual improvement over 6–8 weeks; adherence to full 12-week course is important. Monitor for gastrointestinal side effects and skin irritation.

prescriptions.name: Melasma
prescriptions.summary: Melasma is an acquired hyperpigmentation disorder characterized by symmetric, blotchy brownish macules on sun-exposed areas, particularly the face. It is more common in females and darker skin types. Management involves photoprotection, topical depigmenting agents, and procedural therapies. Treatment is stepwise and requires long-term maintenance due to high recurrence rates.

prescriptions.name: Sunscreen SPF 50+ (tinted preferred)
prescriptions.sig: Apply daily, reapply every 2-3 hours (indefinite)

prescriptions.name: Hydroquinone 4% + Tretinoin 0.05% + Fluocinolone 0.01% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply thin layer to affected facial areas ONCE daily at bedtime (max 8 weeks)

prescriptions.name: Azelaic acid 15-20% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply twice daily (maintenance after stopping hydroquinone)

prescriptions.name: Kojic acid 2% / Tranexamic acid 3% serum
prescriptions.sig: Apply twice daily (alternative maintenance)

prescriptions.name: Tranexamic acid 250 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 8-12 weeks (refractory cases)

prescriptions.notes: Stepwise approach: Step 1 (all patients): SPF 50+ sunscreen + sun avoidance. Step 2 (first-line): Triple combination cream × 8 weeks. Step 3 (at 8 weeks): If improved → stop hydroquinone → start maintenance (azelaic acid/kojic acid). If not improved → add oral tranexamic acid 250 mg BID. Step 4 (at 12 weeks if inadequate): Consider PRP injections, gentle chemical peels, or low-fluence laser (dermatologist only). Step 5 (long-term): Maintenance cream + daily sunscreen + pulse hydroquinone courses as needed. Assess epidermal vs dermal vs mixed pattern using Wood's lamp. Strict photoprotection is critical for all patients.

prescriptions.name: Acute Cystitis (Pregnant Patient)
prescriptions.summary: Acute cystitis in pregnancy is a common bacterial infection of the bladder that requires prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent complications such as pyelonephritis and preterm labor. Asymptomatic bacteriuria also requires treatment in pregnancy. Antibiotic selection must consider fetal safety, with fosfomycin and nitrofurantoin as first-line options, avoiding nitrofurantoin near term. Urine culture is essential to guide therapy, and test-of-cure is recommended.

prescriptions.name: Fosfomycin trometamol 3g sachet
prescriptions.sig: Dissolve in 50-100 ml water. Take as a single dose NOW.

prescriptions.name: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule twice daily for 7 days (if fosfomycin unavailable; avoid at term 38-42 weeks)

prescriptions.name: Cephalexin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule four times daily for 7 days (second-line if nitrofurantoin contraindicated)

prescriptions.notes: LABORATORY: Urine culture (midstream) – send NOW; Test-of-cure urine culture 1-2 weeks after treatment completion. REFER IF: Fever >38°C, flank pain, no improvement after 48 hours, vomiting. Single-dose fosfomycin has the highest cure rate for acute cystitis. Nitrofurantoin is safe in pregnancy but contraindicated at term (38-42 weeks) due to risk of neonatal hemolysis. Cephalexin is a safe second-line option. Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy must also be treated. Hydration and urinary alkalinization may provide symptomatic relief. Consider admission for parenteral antibiotics if pyelonephritis suspected.

prescriptions.name: Acute Tonsillitis (Pregnant - Penicillin Allergy)
prescriptions.summary: Acute tonsillitis in pregnancy is an inflammatory infection of the palatine tonsils, commonly caused by group A Streptococcus (GAS). For penicillin-allergic pregnant patients without anaphylactic reaction, cephalexin is the first-line alternative. Erythromycin is the preferred macrolide in pregnancy due to extensive safety data. Azithromycin may be used if other options are unavailable. Supportive care with paracetamol, saline gargles, and hydration is essential. Monitor for complications and refer for suppurative complications or airway compromise.

prescriptions.name: Cephalexin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule FOUR times daily (every 6 hours) for 7-10 days (Pregnancy Category B)

prescriptions.name: Erythromycin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet FOUR times daily for 7-10 days (Pregnancy Category B)

prescriptions.name: Azithromycin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet ONCE daily for 3 days (use only if cephalexin and erythromycin unavailable)

prescriptions.name: Paracetamol 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: As needed for pain/fever (safe in pregnancy)

prescriptions.name: Warm saline gargles
prescriptions.sig: 3 times daily for symptomatic relief

prescriptions.followUp: 5-7 days (if no improvement, consider throat swab and culture)
prescriptions.notes: EXPECTED OUTCOME: 24-48 hours: Significant symptom improvement; 7-10 days: Complete resolution. REFER IF: Difficulty breathing or stridor, inability to swallow saliva (drooling), muffled voice (hot potato voice), unilateral tonsillar swelling pushing uvula, fever >39°C for >48 hours, dehydration. Cephalexin is first-line for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy (safe, Category B). Erythromycin is the preferred macrolide in pregnancy with most documented experience. Azithromycin is not first-line for Strep pyogenes but can be used if other options unavailable. Emphasize rest and hydration. Consider throat swab for culture if no improvement at 5-7 days.

prescriptions.name: Scabies
prescriptions.summary: Scabies is a highly contagious parasitic infestation caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, characterized by intense nocturnal pruritus and burrows in interdigital spaces, wrists, and flexural areas. Diagnosis is clinical, with burrow identification and family history being key. Treatment involves topical permethrin 5% cream as first-line, with ivermectin for refractory or crusted cases. All household contacts must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfestation. Environmental decontamination is essential for cure.

prescriptions.name: Permethrin 5% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply to entire body from neck to toes (including under nails, between fingers/toes, groin, buttocks, soles). Leave 8-12 hours. Wash off. Repeat after 7 days.

prescriptions.name: Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg
prescriptions.sig: Single dose (weight-based). Repeat after 7-14 days if needed (for refractory/crusted scabies).

prescriptions.name: Cetirizine 10 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet daily for 2-4 weeks (for itching)

prescriptions.followUp: 2 weeks (assess response), 4 weeks (if no improvement, reassess)
prescriptions.notes:
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: Atopic dermatitis (no burrows, flexural distribution, less nocturnal itch); Papular urticaria (insect bites, no burrows); Contact dermatitis (exposure history, sharp borders); Pediculosis (lice visible); Prurigo nodularis (chronic, excoriated nodules).

ENVIRONMENTAL: Hot water wash (≥50°C/122°F) for bedding, clothes, towels; Seal non-washable items in plastic bag for 1 week; Vacuum carpets and furniture; Treat all household contacts simultaneously.

REFER IF: Crusted scabies, immunocompromised patient, no improvement after 2 cycles, secondary bacterial infection.

EXPECTED OUTCOME: Mites killed after 1st application; Pruritus resolves in 2-4 weeks; Complete cure after 2 applications (days 1 and 7-14).

KEY POINTS: All household contacts must be treated simultaneously regardless of symptoms. Permethrin is safe in pregnancy and children >2 months. Ivermectin is pregnancy category C. Pruritus may persist for 2-4 weeks due to hypersensitivity reaction even after successful treatment.

prescriptions.name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
prescriptions.summary: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an infection of the upper female genital tract, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries, typically caused by ascending organisms from the lower tract (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and anaerobic bacteria). Classic presentation includes bilateral lower abdominal pain, adnexal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Prompt antibiotic treatment is essential to prevent complications such as infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. Empiric broad-spectrum therapy covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes is recommended. Treatment should be initiated empirically in sexually active young women with pelvic pain and no other identifiable cause.

prescriptions.name: Ceftriaxone 1g IM
prescriptions.sig: Single dose

prescriptions.name: Doxycycline 100 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

prescriptions.name: Metronidazole 400 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

prescriptions.name: Levofloxacin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 14 days

prescriptions.name: Metronidazole 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

prescriptions.name: Moxifloxacin 400 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 14 days (if M. genitalium suspected)

prescriptions.name: Cefoxitin 2g IM
prescriptions.sig: Single dose

prescriptions.name: Probenecid 1g oral
prescriptions.sig: Single dose

prescriptions.name: Cefotetan 2g IV
prescriptions.sig: Every 12 hours (switch to oral doxycycline after 24-48 hrs), total 14 days

prescriptions.name: Cefoxitin 2g IV
prescriptions.sig: Every 6 hours (switch to oral doxycycline after 24-48 hrs), total 14 days

prescriptions.name: Clindamycin 900mg IV
prescriptions.sig: Every 8 hours (switch to oral doxycycline 100mg BID to complete 14 days)

prescriptions.name: Gentamicin IV/IM
prescriptions.sig: 2mg/kg loading, then 1.5mg/kg every 8 hours (switch to oral doxycycline 100mg BID to complete 14 days)

prescriptions.notes:
REGIMEN A (First-line - Cephalosporin-Based): Ceftriaxone 1g IM single dose + Doxycycline 100mg BID × 14 days + Metronidazole 400mg BID × 14 days.

REGIMEN B (Second-line - Fluoroquinolone-Based): 
- Option 1: Levofloxacin 500mg OD × 14 days + Metronidazole 500mg BID × 14 days
- Option 2: Moxifloxacin 400mg OD × 14 days + Metronidazole 500mg BID × 14 days (if M. genitalium suspected)

REGIMEN C (Third-line - Alternative): Cefoxitin 2g IM single dose + Probenecid 1g oral single dose + Doxycycline 100mg BID × 14 days + Metronidazole 500mg BID × 14 days.

REGIMEN D (Fourth-line - Parenteral/Hospital): 
- Option 1: Cefotetan 2g IV q12h OR Cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + Doxycycline 100mg BID (switch to oral after 24-48 hrs), total 14 days
- Option 2: Clindamycin 900mg IV q8h + Gentamicin 2mg/kg IV/IM loading then 1.5mg/kg IV/IM q8h (switch to oral doxycycline 100mg BID to complete 14 days)

PARTNERS: Treat all partners within 60 days.

REFER IF: No improvement after 72 hours, pregnancy, severe illness, tubo-ovarian abscess, or inability to tolerate oral medications.

ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: 
- Screen for HIV, syphilis, and other STIs
- Counsel on safe sex practices and contraception
- Avoid sexual intercourse until treatment completed and symptoms resolved
- Consider pregnancy test in all reproductive-age women
- Hospitalization criteria: pregnant, severe illness, suspected surgical emergency, tubo-ovarian abscess, inability to tolerate oral medications, or lack of response to outpatient therapy
- Test of cure not routinely recommended for chlamydia/gonorrhea unless symptoms persist or pregnancy
- Repeat testing for chlamydia/gonorrhea recommended in 3-6 months due to high reinfection rates
- Consider IUD removal if symptoms persist after 72 hours

prescriptions.name: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB-O - Ovulatory Dysfunction)
prescriptions.summary: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) is a common gynecological condition characterized by irregular, heavy, or prolonged menstrual bleeding in the absence of structural pathology. In ovulatory dysfunction (AUB-O), bleeding results from anovulation or oligo-ovulation, leading to unopposed estrogen stimulation and endometrial instability. Diagnosis is clinical with normal pelvic exam and negative pregnancy test. Medical management focuses on controlling acute bleeding, regulating menstrual cycles, and preventing recurrence. The combination of tranexamic acid and combined oral contraceptives is highly effective, with tranexamic acid reducing blood loss by 40-60%.

prescriptions.name: Tranexamic Acid 500mg
prescriptions.sig: 1-2 tablets (500-1000mg) three times daily for 3-5 days during menses (reduces blood loss by 40-60%)

prescriptions.name: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (ethinyl estradiol 30-35mcg + progestin)
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet daily for 3-6 months (regulates cycle, prevents recurrence)

prescriptions.name: Ferrous Sulfate 200mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 3 months (treats iron deficiency anemia)

prescriptions.name: Folic Acid 5mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 3 months

prescriptions.name: Paracetamol 500mg
prescriptions.sig: As needed for dysmenorrhea (painful periods)

prescriptions.notes:
CLUES: Irregular heavy/prolonged bleeding + no structural cause + anovulatory pattern + normal pelvic exam + negative pregnancy test.

BEST SINGLE PRESCRIPTION (Highest Cure Rate): Tranexamic Acid 500mg - 1-2 tablets (500-1000mg) TID for 3-5 days during menses + Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (ethinyl estradiol 30-35mcg + progestin) - 1 tablet daily for 3-6 months.

SUPPORTIVE THERAPY: Ferrous Sulfate 200mg BID for 3 months (treats iron deficiency anemia) + Folic Acid 5mg OD for 3 months + Paracetamol 500mg as needed for dysmenorrhea.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: Structural causes (fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis), coagulopathies, thyroid dysfunction, endometrial hyperplasia/malignancy, pregnancy complications, infection.

ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS:
- Rule out pregnancy with serum/urine hCG
- Evaluate for iron deficiency anemia with complete blood count and ferritin
- Consider pelvic ultrasound to exclude structural pathology
- Endometrial biopsy indicated in women >45 years or with risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, PCOS, chronic anovulation, tamoxifen use)
- Lifestyle modifications: weight management if obese, regular exercise
- NSAIDs (mefenamic acid, ibuprofen) can also reduce menstrual blood loss by 20-30%
- Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (Mirena) is an excellent long-term option for heavy menstrual bleeding
- If bleeding persists despite medical therapy, consider endometrial ablation or hysterectomy
- Screen for thyroid disorders and coagulopathies (von Willebrand disease) in appropriate patients

prescriptions.name: H. pylori Infection in Pregnancy
prescriptions.summary: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection in pregnancy requires careful management when treatment is indicated, such as in cases of severe hyperemesis gravidarum, active peptic ulcer disease, or documented infection with significant symptoms. Treatment decisions must balance maternal benefits against potential fetal risks, with antibiotic selection guided by trimester. Dual therapy with amoxicillin and a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) is the preferred first-line regimen across all trimesters due to its safety profile. Triple therapy with metronidazole is reserved for second/third trimester if dual therapy fails. Eradication of H. pylori may improve pregnancy outcomes, including resolution of hyperemesis and reduction of anemia.

prescriptions.name: Amoxicillin 1000mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet three times daily for 14 days
prescriptions.regimen: First Trimester (or preferred for all trimesters)

prescriptions.name: Omeprazole 40mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule twice daily for 14 days
prescriptions.regimen: First Trimester (or preferred for all trimesters)

prescriptions.name: Esomeprazole 40mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule twice daily for 14 days
prescriptions.regimen: First Trimester (or preferred for all trimesters)

prescriptions.name: Metronidazole 500mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days (use ONLY if Amoxicillin + PPI dual therapy has failed, and confirm patient is past first trimester)
prescriptions.regimen: Second/Third Trimester (Alternative if dual therapy fails)

prescriptions.followUp: 4-6 weeks post-treatment (test of cure with stool antigen or urea breath test)
prescriptions.notes:
INDICATIONS: Pregnant patient with confirmed H. pylori + severe hyperemesis OR active peptic ulcer bleeding where benefit of treatment outweighs risk.

FIRST TRIMESTER (or preferred for all trimesters): Amoxicillin 1000mg TID × 14 days + Omeprazole 40mg (or Esomeprazole 40mg) BID × 14 days.

SECOND/THIRD TRIMESTER (Alternative if dual therapy fails): Amoxicillin 1000mg TID × 14 days + Metronidazole 500mg BID × 14 days. Use ONLY if Amoxicillin + PPI dual therapy has failed, and confirm patient is past the first trimester.

SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS:
- Amoxicillin: Pregnancy Category B - safe and preferred
- Omeprazole/Esomeprazole: Pregnancy Category C - use when benefits outweigh risks; limited data but generally considered safe
- Metronidazole: Pregnancy Category B - safe after first trimester; avoid in first trimester
- Clarithromycin: Avoid in pregnancy (Category C, associated with miscarriage risk)
- Tetracycline: Contraindicated in pregnancy (Category D)

OBSTETRIC CONSIDERATIONS:
- H. pylori infection is associated with hyperemesis gravidarum, iron deficiency anemia, and preeclampsia
- Eradication may improve nausea/vomiting in hyperemesis patients
- Screen for iron deficiency anemia as H. pylori can cause occult blood loss
- Consider testing for H. pylori in patients with refractory hyperemesis or unexplained anemia
- Counsel on dietary modifications: avoid spicy foods, caffeine, alcohol, and smoking
- Consider testing and treating household members if recurrent infection
- Retreatment options if eradication fails: consider clarithromycin-based triple therapy (postpartum) or bismuth-based quadruple therapy
- Symptom improvement expected within 1-2 weeks; complete resolution after 14-day course
- If no improvement after 72 hours, reassess for treatment failure or alternative diagnosis

REFER IF: Severe hyperemesis requiring hospitalization, active gastrointestinal bleeding, weight loss, failure to respond to therapy, or need for endoscopic evaluation

prescriptions.name: Acute Diarrhea in Children (<5 years)
prescriptions.summary: Acute diarrhea in children under 5 years is defined as ≥3 loose or watery stools in 24 hours, lasting <14 days. The leading cause is viral (rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus), though bacterial (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter) and parasitic (Giardia) causes should be considered in severe cases or those with dysentery. Management is stepwise based on dehydration severity: Plan A (no dehydration - home care with ORS, zinc, and continued feeding), Plan B (some dehydration - 75 ml/kg ORS over 4 hours in OPD), and Plan C (severe dehydration - IV Ringer's Lactate with hospital referral). Zinc supplementation for 14 days reduces duration and recurrence. Antibiotics are reserved for dysentery or severe bacterial infection. Loperamide is contraindicated in children.

prescriptions.name: ORS (Low-osmolarity) sachets
prescriptions.sig: 1 sachet in 1 liter boiled cooled water. Give 50-100 ml after each loose stool (Plan A - No Dehydration)

prescriptions.name: Zinc sulfate 20mg/5ml syrup
prescriptions.sig: 2.5 ml (10mg) once daily for 14 days (for 1 year old; 20mg daily for children >6 months)

prescriptions.name: Racecadotril 10mg sachet
prescriptions.sig: 1 sachet three times daily for 3 days (if available - reduces stool output)

prescriptions.name: ORS - Plan B (Some Dehydration)
prescriptions.sig: 75 ml/kg over 4 hours (e.g., 750 ml for 10 kg child) - sips every 5-10 minutes

prescriptions.name: IV Ringer's Lactate
prescriptions.sig: 100 ml/kg total: <12 months: 30 ml/kg over 1 hr, then 70 ml/kg over 5 hrs; >12 months: 30 ml/kg over 30 min, then 70 ml/kg over 2.5 hrs

prescriptions.name: Azithromycin 200mg/5ml suspension
prescriptions.sig: 10-20 mg/kg once daily for 3-5 days (for dysentery or bacterial infection)

prescriptions.name: Ciprofloxacin 250mg/5ml suspension
prescriptions.sig: 15 mg/kg/dose twice daily for 3 days (alternative for dysentery)

prescriptions.name: Ceftriaxone IV
prescriptions.sig: 50-80 mg/kg IV once daily (for severe bacterial suspected)

prescriptions.name: Ondansetron
prescriptions.sig: 0.15 mg/kg IV/IM/oral - single dose (for vomiting)

prescriptions.name: Paracetamol
prescriptions.sig: 15 mg/kg every 6 hours PRN fever (avoid ibuprofen with dehydration)

prescriptions.name: Metronidazole
prescriptions.sig: 35-50 mg/kg/day divided TID for 7-10 days (for amebiasis)

prescriptions.followUp: 48 hours (reassess for Plans A & B); immediate for Plan C
prescriptions.notes:
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS & CLUES:
• Viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus, norovirus): Watery diarrhea, vomiting, fever, no blood, self-limiting
• Bacterial gastroenteritis (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter): Bloody diarrhea (dysentery), high fever, abdominal pain, tenesmus
• Amebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica): Bloody diarrhea with mucus ('currant jelly'), no fever or low-grade, chronic
• Giardiasis: Foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea, bloating, flatulence, prolonged course
• Antibiotic-associated diarrhea: History of recent antibiotic use, watery stools, may have C. difficile toxin
• Lactose intolerance: Diarrhea after milk consumption, acidic stools, diaper rash, often post-infectious

KEY MEDICATIONS:
→ ORS - GOLD STANDARD for prevention of dehydration
→ Zinc - ALWAYS (reduces duration and recurrence)
→ Racecadotril - adjunct (reduces stool output)
→ Ondansetron - single dose for vomiting

DO NOT GIVE:
✗ Loperamide (Imodium) - contraindicated in children (dangerous)
✗ Ibuprofen - risk of kidney injury with dehydration
✗ Aspirin - Reye's syndrome
✗ Routine antibiotics - only for dysentery or severe bacterial infection

RED FLAGS (REFER URGENTLY):
□ Blood in stool (dysentery)
□ Severe dehydration (sunken eyes, no urine >6 hours, lethargy, sunken fontanelle)
□ Unable to drink ORS (vomiting everything)
□ Fever >39°C for >48 hours
□ Abdominal distension or severe pain
□ Lethargy or altered consciousness
□ Seizure
□ Malnourished child (SAM) with diarrhea
□ No improvement after 48 hours of treatment

PARENT EDUCATION:
"Your child has diarrhea. The most important treatment is preventing dehydration. Give ORS after every loose stool. Continue feeding your child – do NOT stop milk or food. Give zinc daily for 14 days – this reduces the severity and duration of diarrhea and prevents recurrence. If you see blood in the stool, your child is unable to drink, passes no urine for 6 hours, or becomes very sleepy, bring back immediately. Do NOT give any medicine to stop diarrhea (like Imodium) – these are dangerous for children."

EXPECTED OUTCOME:
→ ORS + Zinc: 3-5 days recovery
→ Add Racecadotril: 24-48 hours faster
→ IV fluids: 1-2 hours improvement
→ Full recovery: 5-7 days

FEEDING GUIDELINES:
✅ Continue breastfeeding or formula
✅ Rice porridge (kanji), mashed banana, khichdi, toast, yogurt (if >6 months)
✅ Small frequent meals
❌ No milk (if >6 months and lactose intolerance suspected – switch to lactose-free)
❌ No juice, soft drinks, sugary water
❌ No solid food for 4-6 hours if vomiting

prescriptions.name: Dysmenorrhea
prescriptions.summary: Dysmenorrhea is defined as painful menstrual cramps of uterine origin, typically beginning 1-2 days before or at the onset of menses, and lasting 1-3 days. It is classified as primary (no underlying pelvic pathology, common in adolescents 6-12 months after menarche) or secondary (associated with pelvic pathology such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID, or IUD). First-line treatment involves NSAIDs started 1-2 days before menses, combined with heat therapy. Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCP) are second-line for moderate-severe cases or when NSAIDs are insufficient. Secondary dysmenorrhea requires investigation with pelvic ultrasound and referral to gynecology.

prescriptions.name: Mefenamic Acid 500mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet three times daily with food. Start 1-2 days before menses, continue for 3-5 days.

prescriptions.name: Ibuprofen 400mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet three times daily with food. Start 1-2 days before menses, continue for 3-5 days.

prescriptions.name: Naproxen 500mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily with food. Start 1-2 days before menses, continue for 3-5 days.

prescriptions.name: Diclofenac Sodium 50mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet three times daily with food. Start 1-2 days before menses, continue for 3-5 days.

prescriptions.name: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (COCP)
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet daily for 21-28 days. Duration: 3-6 cycles (then reassess). Indicated if NSAIDs insufficient.

prescriptions.name: Vitamin E 400 IU
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule daily during menses for 3-5 days (supportive therapy)

prescriptions.name: Magnesium 200mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet daily for 3 months (supportive therapy)

prescriptions.name: Heat therapy (hot water bottle)
prescriptions.sig: Apply to lower abdomen during menses

prescriptions.followUp: 3 cycles (assess response to NSAIDs/COCP); 3 months (assess response to supportive therapy)
prescriptions.notes:
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS & CLUES:
• Endometriosis: Chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, infertility, pain unrelated to menses
• Adenomyosis: Heavy menstrual bleeding, enlarged boggy uterus, pain throughout cycle
• Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): Fever, cervical motion tenderness, abnormal vaginal discharge, bilateral adnexal tenderness
• Ovarian cyst (ruptured/hemorrhagic): Sudden onset of unilateral pain, may have nausea/vomiting, acute abdomen
• Ectopic pregnancy: Amenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, unilateral pain, positive pregnancy test
• Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): Pain related to defecation, altered bowel habit, bloating
• Urinary tract infection (cystitis): Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, positive urine dipstick
• Mittelschmerz: Mid-cycle (ovulation) pain, unilateral, brief duration (hours), no menstrual bleeding

RED FLAGS (REFER FOR SECONDARY CAUSES):
□ No response to NSAIDs or COCP after 3-6 cycles
□ Pain onset >25 years of age (suggests secondary cause)
□ Pain lasting >3 days
□ Pain with intercourse (dyspareunia) – suggests endometriosis
□ Irregular menstrual bleeding (intermenstrual, postcoital, heavy)
□ Abnormal pelvic exam (tenderness, masses, nodules)
□ Infertility
□ Fever or abnormal vaginal discharge (PID)
□ Symptoms of anemia (fatigue, pallor, dizziness) – suggests menorrhagia

DO NOT GIVE:
✗ Opioids for primary dysmenorrhea (ineffective, addictive)
✗ NSAIDs in patients with peptic ulcer or renal disease
✗ COCP in patients with contraindications (>35 years + smoking, migraine with aura, thromboembolic risk, uncontrolled hypertension, breast cancer)

EXPECTED OUTCOME:
→ NSAIDs: Pain relief within 30-60 minutes
→ COCP: 60-90% reduction in pain after 3-6 cycles
→ Full response: 1-2 months

PARENT EDUCATION:
"Dysmenorrhea is painful menstrual cramps caused by prostaglandins – chemicals that make the uterus contract. The pain is real and treatable. Start taking the painkiller 1-2 days BEFORE your period is expected – this is more effective than waiting for pain to start. Take it with food to prevent stomach upset. Apply a hot water bottle to your lower abdomen – this relaxes the uterus and reduces pain. Regular exercise and a healthy diet can reduce the severity of cramps over time. If the pain does not improve after 3-6 cycles, or if you have pain between periods, pain with intercourse, or heavy bleeding, come back – we may need to investigate for other causes."

NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL OPTIONS:
□ Regular aerobic exercise (20-30 min, 3-4 times/week)
□ Dietary modifications: reduce salt, caffeine, alcohol; increase fruits, vegetables
□ Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) – some evidence for pain relief
□ Acupuncture – limited evidence
□ Stress reduction – cognitive behavioral therapy, relaxation techniques
□ Vitamin D supplementation – if deficiency present
□ Fish oil (omega-3) – anti-inflammatory effect (modest benefit)

prescriptions.name: Pregnancy Constipation
prescriptions.summary: Constipation in pregnancy is a common condition defined as infrequent bowel movements (<3 per week), hard stools, and straining, affecting up to 40% of pregnant women. It is caused by hormonal changes (increased progesterone), mechanical compression by the growing uterus, and iron supplementation. First-line treatment involves lifestyle modifications (increased fiber, hydration, exercise) and fiber supplements. Polyethylene Glycol 3350 (PEG) is the preferred osmotic laxative as it is minimally absorbed and safe in pregnancy. Lactulose is a safe alternative. Bulk-forming agents like psyllium require adequate water to avoid obstruction. Stimulant laxatives and mineral oil should be strictly avoided due to safety concerns.

prescriptions.name: Polyethylene Glycol 3350 (PEG) 17g powder
prescriptions.sig: 1 sachet (17g) dissolved in 250-500ml water ONCE daily. Duration: 2-4 weeks, then reassess. Preferred by ACOG and AGA. Onset: 24-72 hours.

prescriptions.name: Lactulose 10g/15ml syrup
prescriptions.sig: 15-30ml (10-20g) ONCE daily. Duration: 2-4 weeks. Alternative if PEG unavailable. Onset: 24-48 hours.

prescriptions.name: Psyllium husk (Ispaghol) 6g
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablespoon in 1 glass of water ONCE daily. Must be taken with adequate water to avoid obstruction.

prescriptions.name: Docusate Sodium 100mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily (stool softener – considered safe if second-line fails after 1-2 weeks)

prescriptions.notes:
STEPWISE APPROACH:

FIRST LINE (Lifestyle + Fiber):
□ Increase fiber intake to 25-30g daily (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes)
□ Drink 8-12 cups (2-3 liters) of water daily
□ Daily walking or exercise (20-30 minutes)
□ Regular toileting routine (especially after meals)
□ Psyllium husk 6g daily (if dietary fiber insufficient)

SECOND LINE (If first-line fails):
□ ADD Polyethylene Glycol 3350 17g daily (preferred)
□ OR Lactulose 15-30ml daily (alternative)

THIRD LINE (If second-line fails after 1-2 weeks):
□ ADD Docusate Sodium 100mg twice daily (stool softener)

STRICTLY AVOID:
✗ Castor oil – uterine stimulation risk
✗ Mineral oil – reduced vitamin absorption, risk of neonatal bleeding
✗ Senna – contraindicated due to genotoxicity concerns
✗ Magnesium citrate/sodium phosphate – risk of electrolyte imbalance

RED FLAGS (REFER URGENTLY):
□ No bowel movement for 1 week despite treatment
□ Severe abdominal pain
□ Rectal bleeding
□ Fever
□ Signs of obstruction (vomiting, distension, no flatus)

PATIENT EDUCATION:
"Constipation is very common in pregnancy due to hormonal changes and the growing baby pressing on your bowel. The safest approach is to increase your fiber intake and drink plenty of water. If that doesn't work, the powder laxative (PEG) is the preferred treatment during pregnancy – it works by drawing water into your bowel and is not absorbed into your body. Do NOT use castor oil or mineral oil – these are unsafe in pregnancy. If you have severe pain, bleeding, or no bowel movement for a week, come back immediately."

EXPECTED OUTCOME:
→ Lifestyle changes + fiber: Improvement in 2-7 days
→ PEG or Lactulose: Bowel movement in 24-72 hours
→ Full response: 1-2 weeks with consistent treatment

ADDITIONAL NOTES:
- Constipation is most common in the first and third trimesters
- Iron supplements can worsen constipation – consider switching to a different formulation or reducing dose
- Probiotics may have a modest benefit
- Women with a history of constipation or pelvic floor dysfunction are at higher risk

prescriptions.name: Neuropathic Pain (Peripheral Neuropathy)
prescriptions.summary: Peripheral neuropathy is a length-dependent, stocking-glove distribution of nerve damage characterized by burning pain, tingling, numbness, and night worsening. Common causes include diabetes mellitus, vitamin B12 deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, uremia, and drug toxicity. First-line treatment according to NICE guidelines includes pregabalin, gabapentin, or duloxetine, chosen based on patient profile and comorbidities. Treatment requires gradual titration and 4-6 weeks to assess response. Secondary causes must be investigated and treated simultaneously. Specialist referral is needed for refractory cases, rapidly progressive weakness, or autonomic involvement.

prescriptions.name: Pregabalin 75mg
prescriptions.sig: Start 75mg at bedtime for 7 days, then 75mg twice daily for 7 days, then 150mg twice daily. Max 600mg/day. Duration: 4-6 weeks, then reassess.

prescriptions.name: Gabapentin 100mg
prescriptions.sig: Start 100mg three times daily. Increase weekly: 300mg TID, 600mg TID, 900mg TID. Max 3600mg/day. Duration: 4-6 weeks, then reassess.

prescriptions.name: Duloxetine 30mg
prescriptions.sig: 30mg once daily for 7 days, then increase to 60mg once daily. Max 120mg/day. Duration: 4-6 weeks, then reassess. Indicated for neuropathic pain with depression, diabetic neuropathy.

prescriptions.name: Amitriptyline 10-25mg
prescriptions.sig: Start 10-25mg at bedtime. Increase by 10-25mg weekly. Max 75mg/day. Duration: 4-6 weeks, then reassess.

prescriptions.name: Tramadol 50mg
prescriptions.sig: 50mg 3-4 times daily. Max 400mg/day. Short-term use only (<4 weeks).

prescriptions.name: Vitamin B Complex
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 3 months

prescriptions.name: Alpha-lipoic acid 600mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule once daily for 3 months (modest benefit in diabetic neuropathy)

prescriptions.name: Methylcobalamin 1500mcg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 1 month, then 1500mcg once weekly for 2 months (for Vitamin B12 deficiency)

prescriptions.name: Topical Capsaicin 0.075% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply to painful areas 3-4 times daily

prescriptions.followUp: 2 weeks (assess pain reduction, side effects, dose titration); 4-6 weeks (reassess pain levels, switch or combine if inadequate); 3 months (repeat NCS if initially abnormal, review cause treatment)
prescriptions.notes:
DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP (Must Rule Out Causes):
• Diabetes mellitus: HbA1c, Fasting Blood Sugar (FBS)
• Vitamin B12 deficiency: Vitamin B12 level
• Alcohol: LFTs, history
• Hypothyroidism: TSH, T4
• Uremia: Creatinine, BUN
• Drugs: Medication history (isoniazid, metronidazole, vincristine, amiodarone)
• Inflammatory: Nerve conduction study (NCS) if uncertain

RED FLAGS (REFER URGENTLY):
□ Rapidly progressive weakness (Guillain-Barré, CIDP)
□ Asymmetric neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex)
□ Autonomic symptoms (orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, erectile dysfunction)
□ Unexplained weight loss or fever
□ History of cancer or neurotoxic drug exposure
□ Bowel/bladder dysfunction
□ No improvement after 6 weeks of first-line therapy

CAUSE-SPECIFIC TREATMENT:
• Diabetic Neuropathy: Tight glycemic control (HbA1c <7%) + Gabapentin or Duloxetine
• Vitamin B12 Deficiency: Methylcobalamin 1500mcg daily for 1 month, then weekly for 2 months
• Alcohol-Related Neuropathy: Stop alcohol + Thiamine 100mg daily + Folic acid 5mg daily for 1 month

EXPECTED OUTCOME:
→ 2 weeks: Initial response
→ 4-6 weeks: Full effect
→ 3 months: Reassess and adjust

PATIENT EDUCATION:
"You have nerve pain (neuropathy). This is caused by damaged nerves sending false pain signals to your brain. The burning and tingling you feel is NOT in your imagination – it is real nerve pain. The medicine I am prescribing works by calming down the overactive nerves. It takes 2-4 weeks to work fully. Start with a low dose and increase gradually as I have instructed. Do NOT stop suddenly – this can cause withdrawal symptoms. If you feel dizzy or sleepy, increase the dose more slowly and take it at bedtime. We must find the cause of your neuropathy. I am ordering blood tests to check for diabetes, B12 deficiency, and thyroid problems. Treating the cause is as important as treating the pain."

DO NOT GIVE:
✗ NSAIDs – ineffective for neuropathic pain
✗ Opioids as first-line – limited efficacy, risk of dependence
✗ Corticosteroids – unless inflammatory cause confirmed
